 I mostly use my TCL Google TV for gaming and I love it. But it wasn’t as fun while watching movies. At times, I’d notice the movie stutter for half a second. My first instinct was blaming my Wi-Fi, but I couldn’t have been more wrong. The real issue was a mismatch between frame rates, and since it only stuttered during specific scenes, it took me a while to realize it. Once I figured that out, though, the actual fix took barely 30 seconds.

 Mismatched frame rates were causing the stutter
 It wasn’t my Wi-Fi

 Stuttering happens when a frame stays on the screen for too long. It’s one of those things that’s easy to notice, and there’s a simple reason why it happens.
 Movies and TV shows are shot at 24 frames per second. That’s been the cinematic standard for almost a century now. Modern TVs obviously don’t run at 24Hz. They run at 60Hz, and some even go up to 120Hz. So you’ve got content built around one frame rate trying to play on a display built around a completely different one. And that mismatch is exactly where the stutter comes from.
 This is not some new problem, of course. TVs have a trick to deal with this called 3:2 pulldown. They show one frame three times and the other twice to stretch 24 frames to 60 seconds. Since 60 isn’t even divisible by 24, the 3:2 pulldown manages frames this way:
 Frame 1 for 3 refresh cycles
 Frame 2 for 2 refresh cycles
 Frame 3 for 3 refresh cycles
 Frame 4 for 2 refresh cycles
 The math works out, and your TV is able to show the same movie on a 60Hz screen. It’s a clever workaround, and most of the time, it works great. But sometimes, this uneven display pattern can create judder, especially during slow camera pans and horizontal movement. That’s when it doesn’t play out well and your eyes catch that stutter.
 I wasn’t familiar with any of this when I first noticed stuttering on my TV, so naturally, I blamed my Wi-Fi and the streaming apps I was using . I tried everything to fix the internet connection too, from restarting my modem to checking network settings, before I finally realized the mismatched frame rates were what caused the stutter all along.
 Enabling frame rate matching fixed it for me
 TV manufacturers should pre-enable this
 Pankil Shah / MUO 
 Fixing all that stuttering on my TV turned out to be embarrassingly simple. My TCL TV had a toggle to fix this the entire time. I just didn’t know what it was.
 Most TVs have an option called frame rate matching. Different TVs label this option differently, but they do the same thing. Instead of forcing 24fps content through that 3:2 pulldown trick to fit a 60Hz panel, the TV switches its own output to match the source. So when a movie plays at 24fps, the TV actually outputs at 24Hz, or a multiple of it, like 48Hz or 120Hz.
 This eliminates the need for a pulldown pattern completely, because the TV doesn’t have to force a mismatch to work. It’s just displaying frames at the rate they’re meant to be shown. On my TCL TV, it was under Settings > Display and sound > Match content frame rate . There were two options here: Seamless and Non-seamless .
 Seamless switches the refresh rate without any visual disruption, so the screen doesn’t flicker or go black when the frame rate changes. Non-seamless does the same thing of matching content frame rate, but the screen does briefly cut out while the TV adjusts. You can pick the one you like, but the important thing here is that not every TV has this feature. So yes, if you don’t see any similarly labelled option on your TV’s display settings, it might not support it. The other thing is that the streaming app you’re using also needs to support it.
 Enabling filmmaker mode can help too
 Another thing you can do to make your movie experience better is enable Filmmaker Mode from Display settings. It’s something most TVs include these days, and it basically helps preserve the content the way it was shot.
 The main thing it does is turn off motion smoothing , that soap-opera effect that makes movies look unnaturally fluid. Motion smoothing works by inserting artificial frames between the real ones to make motion look smoother. It’s essentially your TV guessing what should go between two real frames to smooth out that difference between 24fps and 60fps. Since these guessed frame aren’t real, that can sometimes ruin your movie experience.
 Filmmaker Mode doesn’t fix the mismatched frame rate the way the above feature does, but it does stop your TV from messing with the signal, which can help with judder.
